newsitem.title: USA: World Bank will end any corruption-tainted projects.
newsitem.headline: World Bank will end any corruption-tainted projects.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn, adding teeth to his attack on global corruption, vowed on Thursday to pull out of any project funded by his institution that proved to be tainted by wrongdoing.

"Where there are projects to which we are involved and we find evidence of corruption we will cancel the project," he told reporters. "We are anxious to put teeth into what we're doing over issues in which we have control."
Both Wolfensohn and International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus have focused a bright light on corruption during the annual meetings of the IMF and Bank that ended on Thursday.
The World Bank chief said graft and other practices are a major barrier to economic progress in developing nations.

Moreover, corruption threatened to rob the Bank of support in industrial countries as governments -- and the voters who elect them -- wonder if the money they have contributed is ending up in the pockets of corrupt officials.
Wolfensohn argued that governments that fight corruption will find that their economies will become more attractive to vital foreign investment.
Camdessus also took aim at these practices during a speech to the plenary session, saying governments must demonstrate that they have no tolerance for corruption in any form.
The World Bank and the IMF lend tens of billions of dollars to developing countries each year, giving added weight to their admonishments about the bribery and corruption.
The World Bank board recently set up new procurement guidelines for projects financed by its loans -- action which U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin has applauded.

Under the guidelines, the Bank can cancel part of a loan if it determines that corrupt or fraudulent practices were involved in procurement contracts. It can also bar guilty companies from bidding on future bank-financed projects.

During his final press conference, Wolfensohn conceded that the Bank could not become a moral policeman or interfere in the political independence of countries. Nor, he said, would such efforts change human behaviour overnight.
"The bank will not interfere in the political sphere...but we can try to create a climate in which people fight corruption," he said. "The bank cannot run countries."

But he said that by putting the glare of publicity on the problem, pressure could be generated within countries to make changes. Already, he said, there had been a strong positive reaction from a number of countries.

"There has been a very, very strong measure of support for our efforts ... a unity in the international community from both donor and recipient countries," he said in closing address to the plenary session.

Wolfensohn made clear he was not playing any favourites. He noted that corruption was a worldwide problem in which wealthy industrial countries, in their efforts to do business in the developing world, had added to the climate of loose practices.
"As one of the (Bank) governors said, you have a corrupted and you have a corruptee," he told reporters.
